newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Shanghai begins cautious sale of state firms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Shanghai begins cautious sale of state firms.

text.p: Two years ago Zhao Honggen was chief of a debt-ridden state factory making wooden beds that many people believed had no future.
But Zhao and his workers decided to buy the plant from the state and today he is director and principal shareholder. Business has grown and healthy profits are expected for 1996.
The Shanghai Masses Wooden Instruments Factory is one of about 90 small and medium-sized state firms in China's biggest manufacturing city that have been sold to their workers as an experiment.
About 10,000 other companies in Shanghai alone are waiting in the wings to see if the experiment succeeds.

But advocates of such sell-offs say that the city is moving too slowly, because of opposition from officials wary of shedding state assets and from factory chiefs who do not want to leave the state sector.
Zhao at the Wooden Instruments Factory is not one of them.
"The factory's business started to decline in 1988 and our debts mounted," he said in an interview. "We had too little capital and our products were out-of-date."
FOLLOWING SUIT
"By 1994 we had to borrow money from anywhere we could to pay the wages. We did not know what to do."
That year, a state factory making lanterns in Shanghai was sold to its employees, the first case of its kind in the city.
Zhao and his colleagues decided to follow suit, arguing that workers who had a stake in their firm would work much harder than those who merely collected a wage each month.

So far the sell-off has worked. Sales in 1996 are estimated at 18 million yuan, up from 15 million in 1995 and four million in 1994, with the company's product range broadened to include mahogany furniture for home and offices.

It has moved its furniture production to the outskirts of the city and rented out most of its factory space as offices. It also plans to turn two storeys of the main factory building into a hotel and restaurant.

The initial success of Zhao's firm and 13 others that have been sold off could point the way for the other 10,000 small and medium-sized state-run firms in Shanghai, mostly shops and service establishments. At least a third lose money.
There are several reasons why so few companies have been sold off, said Ge Xiulu, an economist and one of Shanghai's leading advocates of shareholding co-operatives.

One reason is that the heads of most firms do not want to take the risk, preferring to remain within the comparative safety of the state system, with employment, credit and welfare benefits more or less guaranteed.
"MISGUIDED THINKING"
Another is that officials want to sell off only state firms that are losing money -- which their workers generally don't want to buy -- because they fear a loss of state assets.

"This is misguided thinking," Ge said in an interview. "It is not a loss to the state, since the state receives money from the sale and is relieved of the burden of having to support that company in the future."

In the case of the furniture firm, the workers bought it from the state for one million yuan, with production staff paying 3,000 to 6,000 yuan each and Zhao paying 20,000, making him the biggest shareholder with two percent of the shares.
"It took more than a month to persuade the workers that it was worth buying into the firm," Zhao said. "Three left because they thought the company had no hope."
The firm has prospered because it has diversified into office and household furniture at a time when the city is in the middle of a building boom.
In addition, its central location means it can easily find tenants for spare space.
Zhao expects to earn about 11,000 yuan this year, plus a dividend of 4,000 yuan, more than double the total of 7,200 yuan he took home in wages in 1994.

"But I have a level of pressure I never had running a state firm," Zhao said. "Some factory chiefs do not want to try this as there is too much pressure and risk. If you run a state firm, it does not matter whether you earn or lose money."
